comments.author: jacobgold
comments.text: First, congrats to the team on launching something genuinely interesting and new. Seems like a more accurate title would be "Jev: Trading general purpose generation for fast typed inference" or something like that. This is interesting, but the speed comparison seems misleading? A generative model that can output code in a Turing-complete language can do anything a computer can do. Jev can only generate structured output, right? This is probably super useful for classification/routing/scoring, but it's nothing like the code generating models we're all using today for code and automation. Also "can't hallucinate" seems wrong? Sure, it can't emit an invalid type, but it can still emit a completely wrong valid value. You can enforce structured output from an LLM too, with an appropriate harness, etc. Assuming there's no funny business, the Doom demo is cool.

comments.author: futurisold
comments.text: This, combined with contracts, could make a lot of things so much fun now! For those who don't know (which is probably everyone but me), I ported the design-by-contract pattern in Python and combined it with LLMs. This was early 2025. I originally wrote about it here: https://leoveanu.com/2025-03-01-dbc/ . Contracts are a core feature of SymbolicAI ever since. The community seems to have loved it too ( https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44399234 ). I think I'm starting to glimpse the implications and it's gonna change agentic workloads if it holds up to scrutiny. It's too early for me to tell anything other than jot down some rough thoughts. In short, you get blazingly fast semantic branching you can use in control flows. For contracts, I can now directly take the data model that you have to design and convert it into Jev's expected format. Or I can use Jev for semantic branching in postconditions. If my understanding is correct, that should be doable, but I need to think more about it. It could be that with Jev I can finally “compile contracts” and better chain them into workflows, which is something I always wanted but didn't know how to do properly. Eager to test. On the waiting list.

comments.author: bregmandiv
comments.text: I'm trying to parse it down to what we had before vs what is new here. We already had encoder models that skipped text generation for giving us a numerical output that could be computed as a probability. we also got no hallucinations and faster inference for free there. So we already had 1. "unstructured state in, probabilistic decisions out" 2. "orders of magnitude faster and more efficient" What was hard there was to train the model head without ML expertise, and considerable amount of data. This seems like this is a democratization of those encoders? The addition over existing encoders seems to be coming from being able to specify the output shape (up to a cardinality of 255). It is unclear to me if this is possible using Jev without additional labels for fine-tuning. If so, that is still very impressive, but I think the faster inference and 0 hallucinations might come for free, from it not being generative.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点: Jevは生成型LLMではなく構造化出力（選択・スコア・ラベルなど）に特化した高速推論エンジンであり、トークンベースの速度比較が誤解を招く点や、「hallucination なし」という主張の正確さが議論された。  
賛否両論: 分類・ルーティング・スコアリングなどの構造化タスクでは爆発的な速度と型安全性を評価する声がある一方、汎用コード生成や複雑な推論には向かず、既存のエンコーダーモデルとの差別化が不明瞭だと指摘する意見もある。  
注目コメント: 一人は設計による契約（DbC）と組み合わせれば、データモデルを直接Jevの形式に変換してワークフローの意味的分岐をコンパイルできる可能性に期待を示し、もう一人はラベル不要で出力形状（最大255クラス）を指定できる点が、従来のエンコーダーを民主化する画期的機能だと強調している。
stories.editor_note: System Oneモデルは推論レイテンシを半分に削減する新アーキテクチャで、伴うツールJevがモデル変換を自動化。急激なLLM利用コスト増に対応する業界の期待が高まっており、国内クラウド事業者のGPU最適化にも直結する可能性がある。

RheinmetallがBattlesuite接続武器システムプロトコルの仕様を公開したこと。記事ではオープンソースと謳われているが、実際にはGitHubにコードがなくドキュメントのみの公開である点、そしてプロトコルがDDSベースであることが議論の中心となった。

stories.summary_ja:
### 主な議論点
コミュニティでは、セルの100歳の誕生日を祝うとともに、彼の数学教育に対する影響や、数学の形式主義（特にε-δ論法）に関する彼の率直な意见が大きく議論された。多くのコメントが、セルの著作や思想が数学を学ぶ人々に与えたポジティブな影響を強調した。特に、抽象的な数学的概念を現実の応用や個人的な経験と結びつける彼の能力が称賛された。

### 賛否両論
コメント全体は賛意に満ちており、明確な賛否両論は見られなかった。しかし、数学の教育方法、特に形式主義の過度な強調に関するcellsの批判は、自身が数学から離れた経験を持つ人々と共鸣を呼んでおり、教育の在り方に関する潜在的な意见の相違をうかがわせた。

### 注目コメント
特に注目されたコメントとして、セルが対称群の線形表現に関する本を、妻の量子化学の研究のため書いたというエピソードが挙げられた。これは、数学が他分野や個人的な関係と深く結びつく例として、 CELの「夫としての責任を果たした」というユーモアTogether with、人間味あふれる側面を印象的に示していた。また、ε-δ論法を嫌い、数学から離れたというcellsの告白は、形式主義に苦手意識を持つ多くの人間と共鸣し、数学教育のあり方を考える上で重要な視点を提供していた。
stories.editor_note: 代数幾何学の巨匠Jean‑Pierre Serreが100歳を迎え、彼の深遠な理論は現在の機械学習における表現学習や代数的手法にも根を下ろしている。日本の大学では彼の著作を教材にし、次世代の理論系研究者育成に活用している。

comments.author: nrmitchi
comments.text: Whether it's valid or not, there is something that rubs me the wrong way about a security tools company using a real customer/vendor as a marketing campaign. This "story" could have been told without naming, bluntly, their "victim". It would be different if it was some complex, multi-step exploit, but the tone is closer to "look how much Baseten fucked up!". Strix also crossed the line at this point: > Strix decided to pull an image and see what was inside. You're going past the white-hat point here when you start active exfiltrating data and looking at it. Once you start using credentials from the exfiltrated data and start listing and poking around internal systems, you are way past it. Listen, I get it, their product is "meant for" self-testing, so it assumes it's safe to go digging. After all, it's a self check. That is exactly why it's irresponsible, and borderline illegal, for them to point it at a third party. Even if they had "permission", I dobut that permission extended to "and also search and/or download our repos if you can". The overall tone is less than professional. Statements like (in bold) "This is an insane amount of access to leave in a publicly downloadable image." Everyone is aware of this, and it's phrase like it was a purposeful decision. Security tools from teams that actively shit on the people they're designed to "help" feels wrong. Edit: For clarity on my point about "pulling repos", this post includes descriptions of the purpose and functionality of multiple repos (which is past what a name gives them), and they explicitly state: "A listing of that private repo showed a top-level customers/ directory, with subdirectory after subdirectory named after Baseten customers". comments.author: sholladay
comments.text: One big problem is that prices are easy to compare, while quality is not. I recently bought a tub that was advertised as stainless steel on Amazon. I was suspicious but decided to take a chance. Turns out it is galvanized, not stainless. I’m not sure the average person knows the difference. To be charitable, perhaps that’s even why the listing advertised it that way. But the difference matters significantly in terms of performance and quality, especially for certain kinds of products and use cases. There’s no “sort by quality, best to worst” system like there is for price. No “genuine stainless only” filter. You just have to know certain things. Shopping in person obviously helps, but you still have to know what to look for. Refrigerators are a good example of this. Most people shop for them in person, yet it’s not at all obvious whether model A or model B will last longer. You can try to use price as a proxy for quality, but the more expensive refrigerators are actually more likely to fail years earlier because of the added component complexity. They’re basically banking on the fact that you don’t know how to read a wiring diagram. To combat that, lots of people turn to YouTube or reviews to figure out quality. And sure, you can find some good sources that will tell you that top freezers will last longer than a French door model at basically any price, and they might even explain why. But all of those platforms are muddied with perverse incentives, affiliate programs, sponsorships, etc. Again, not always obvious. We need to make quality obvious. We need to make it comparable, sortable, filtrable, and guaranteed. Poor design needs to be a valid reason to return an item. Manufacturers should be required to label products with an estimated lifespan. Give tax breaks or other incentives to products that include a warranty for its full lifespan. We have to figure out how to improve the efficiency of making high quality goods, so that everything doesn’t just get more expensive. There should be a public database of the best known designs and techniques for making long lasting items. Patents that relate to longevity could be given extra time to encourage research, but then after, say, 3 years there could be a requirement to license the technology so that it can go mainstream. This doesn’t solve everything. Some products need more specific approaches. Food quality is a problem. Housing needs to be both more affordable and higher quality. But I think with enough changes to incentives, the culture could shift towards seeing the value in making things well.

comments.author: vehemenz
comments.text: The CSS Zen Garden worked because everyone was using a single markup file. In real life, it doesn't really work. Instead of thinking of separation of concerns as a religious principle, think about what benefits it actually yields in the case of HTML. When the markup is completely separated from its styling, this means that the CSS rules need a way to be mapped onto the DOM. This involves specific elements, organized a specific way. If anything is out of place in the markup, the properties may not apply as intended. Similarly, if the CSS doesn't account for DOM structures, then you need modify rules or add new ones. This way of mapping is an implicit structure. It's something extra that's required, beyond the source code that's there. It can be computed by the browser, but it's not explicitly stated for a developer looking at the code to understand. Contrast this with Tailwind, Tachyons, etc., where nearly all the structure is explicit, less complex, discoverable, and out in the open. Hidden structure looks nice to the developer. The code "looks" clean. But understanding a code base's implicit structure is ephemeral, and there's inherent technical debt that will need to be repaid later. Tailwind looks ugly, but there are no hidden abstractions or structures in the code, beyond its easy conventions and a minimal config file. And, yes, there are ways to make high-abstraction CSS work, say, with a component library of known DOM patterns. But at that point, why not build the styles into the components directly, a la Tailwind, instead of adding complexity?

They think the markup/stylesheet separation of concerns was a terrible idea, an idea that Tailwind exists to fix. (I think they're wrong, that separation of concerns is good, Tailwind is a hack, and get off my lawn while you're at it.) The point is - now the modern vanilla web platform really can support first-class CSS-styled app components , from design systems, in production. This is really cool! HTML and CSS were originally designed as document-oriented languages for digital document display; think MS Word or PDF with cross-document hyperlinks, and not an app SDK. The idea was simply "style your web site's titles, headings, paragraphs, footers, etc. in just one place; change it there and the whole site will update". That's the dream that CSS Zen Garden was meant to showcase. Interactivity and web apps came later , and CSS has taken a very long time to catch up. But catch up it has, and I'll be glad when frontend web development sheds Tailwind and React in favor of the updated vanilla web platform; and I won't complain if we use super light web component libraries like Lit[0]). stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、CSS Zen Gardenが示したマークアップとスタイルの完全分離（「スキン変更可能な同じHTML」）が現実のウェブ開発でどれほど機能するかという点。賛側は、関心の分離によりデザインを一元管理でき、サイト全体の一貫した変更が容易で、設計の自由度が高まるとしている。反対側は、実際のマークアップは多様で固定せざるを得ず、スタイルがDOM構造に依存する暗黙の構造が生じ、これが技術的負債になると指摘。また、TailwindなどのユーティリティーファーストCSSはその隠れた構造を露出させ、理解しやすいがクラスの羅列が冗長になるとの意見も。注目コメントとして、最新のCSS（カスタムプロパティ、Flexbox、Grid）とウェブコンポーネントにより、バニラプラットフォームだけで設計システムを実現できるという意見があり、Zen Gardenの夢は過去の幻想ではなく、現代の仕組みで再評価すべきだとする声が挙げられた。
stories.editor_note: かつてのCSS Zen Gardenのように、HTMLは固定しスタイルシートだけで完全に異なるデザインを実現する取り組みが、実際の製品としてリリースされた。これにより、日本のフロントエンド開発者はデザインとロジックの分離を再考し、テーマ切り替えやダークモード対応をCSSのみで行う手法への関心が高まっている。

stories.title_en: Most people prefer traditional architecture

comments.author: hardwaregeek
comments.text: Perhaps there’s a difference between what people prefer looking at and what’s actually nicer to inhabit? Architecture is optimizing for people inhabiting the building, not just staring at it in a photograph. It’s like if you asked someone to judge a phone based on a photo. Yes there’s some aesthetic judgement but it matters more if the phone is usable. I know that personally I find New York’s prewar buildings more beautiful than your average soulless luxury tower. But I enjoyed living in a soulless luxury tower because it had good lighting, not terrible elevators and decent fixtures.

comments.author: boh
comments.text: Modernism is the act of using cheaper resources and more standardized/cheaper methods of production. The aesthetic is more of a side-effect of those limits. Ugliness has become a cultural norm in order to suit the modern economy. It may come as a surprise but it required years of cultural development and education for most people to accept the work of Dieter Rams as some aesthetic pinnacle rather than soulless mass production. It's only recently, (with designs like the Ferrari EV for instance) that people are starting to see how limited our aesthetic language has become. Modernism is too cheap to replace so the "beauty" of soulless minimalism will likely endure in the zeitgeist, but it's not a very interesting environment to be in.

To hide the joints in wood—when columns were made of wood, only these aren’t, they’re marble. The triglyphs, what are they? Wood. Wooden beams, the way they had to be laid when people began to build wooden shacks. Your Greeks took marble and they made copies of their wooden structures out of it, because others had done it that way. Then your masters of the Renaissance came along and made copies in plaster of copies in marble of copies in wood. stories.editor_note: 最近の調査で、応答者の過半数が伝統的様式の建築を現代的ガラスビルよりも好むことが明らかになった。これにより、日本でも歴史的街並みの保存と新築設計における和様式の取り入れが再評価され、観光資源としての価値が見直されている。

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、スマートリングの実用性におけるバッテリー膨張リスク、サイズ調整の不可能さ、手洗い時の着脱の手間、プライバシーとデータ収集への懸念、そしてサブスクリプションモデルや短いバッテリー寿命によるコストパフォーマンスの悪さである。  

賛否両論では、睡眠・HRV・RHRのトラッキング精度は高評価されるものの、バッテリーがすぐに劣化し、高価なデバイスがすぐに電子廃棄物になる点や、月額料金が必要ない機能にも課金される仕組みに批判が集まる。一方で、通常の指輪と同様にサイズ選びや手入れの問題は避けられず、ジムなどで着脱を嫌うユーザーには不向きだと指摘する声もある。また、データがローカルに留まらないことへの不安から、監視型ビジネスモデルに反対する意見も目立つ。  

注目コメントとして、「内部バッテリーが膨張すると危険な状況になる」という警告や、「Ouraリングは優れた睡眠分析を提供するが、バッテリー持続時間とサブスクリプションが駄目で、Garmin時計に乗り換えた」という実体験が挙げられ、機能とコスト・プライバシーのトレードオフが議論の中心となっている。
stories.editor_note: バッテリー持続時間とセンサー精度の限界が顕在化し、消費者の関心がスマートウォッチやイヤホンに移っていることを示すデータが発表された。これにより、日本のウェアラブルスタートアップは、リングよりもヘルスケア向けパッチや衣服組み込み型センサーへの方向転換を検討し始めている。

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、25年にわたる大規模監視が人々に misery をもたらし、さらに悪化する恐れがあることである。コメントでは、老子の言葉を引用して制限が逆効果になると指摘する声、個人所有のデバイスで動くプライバシー保護サービスを広めるべきだと提案する声、監視ネットワークへの連邦アクセスを地方管轄に限定すべきだと主張する声、NSPM-7 が監視をさらに強化すると危惧する声、そして最終的に監視が国家安全保障問題となり敵対勢力にも利用され得るという警告が見られた。賛否については、監視を制限し自分たちでツールを提供しようとする前向きな提案と、監視の拡大は避けられず逆に危険が増すという懐疑的・悲観的な見解に分かれた。特に洞察に富んだコメントとして、老子の「制限はそれを防ぐべき混乱を生む」という引用と、連邦の目の届く範囲を地方に限定する「境界が安定をもたらす」という提案が注目された。
stories.editor_note: 過去25年間の国家レベルの通信監視が、テロ防止への効果が限定的であるとの評価が上がり、プライバシー侵害の是非が再論じられている。日本では、盗聴法改正やマイナンバー制度の見直しにおいて、同様の「十分だ」論点が政策議論に影響を与えている。
